1:
Who Melchizedek was is the question the chapter opens on, and the answers are catalogued at length. Gill canvasses the guesses that he was an angel, the Holy Ghost, or the Son of God himself, and disposes of them all by one argument, that he is said to be made like unto the Son of God and Christ to be of his order, which manifestly distinguishes the two; among those who take him for a mere man he rejects the identification with Shem, the constant opinion of the Jewish writers, since it is not true of Shem that he was without father and without mother, his descent being recorded. Henry reports the same two chief opinions, the rabbinic one for Shem and the one held by many Christian writers that Christ himself appeared to Abraham in the flesh under that name, and answers the first by observing that Shem would hardly have changed his name. Ellicott treats the Shem identification as a Jewish legend preserved in the later Targums but absent from the oldest, and suspects that the whole history of speculation has invested this chapter with a mystery that does not belong to it. Henry answers the difficulty differently: God has thought fit to leave us in the dark precisely that Melchizedek might be the livelier type of one whose generation none can declare, and men who will not be satisfied with what is revealed must rove about in endless conjectures.

Calvin leaves the identification alone and dwells on how remarkable the figure is: when the whole world had fallen into impiety and Abraham's own father and grandfather had degenerated into idolatry, here was a king who not only retained true religion but performed the office of a priest himself. Chrysostom looks instead at the writer's method, that he shoots from afar and prepares beforehand, rebuking his readers as weak and then soothing them, since a man depressed in spirits would not be a ready hearer. Robertson calls it a daring thing to put Melchizedek above Aaron, and grants that the method of interpretation is rabbinical though well adapted to Jewish readers. Ellicott states the aim more soberly: not to allegorise each part of the history, but to draw out the meaning of the comparison the prophecy had made; and he notices what is left out, that of the facts recorded in Genesis none is passed over except the gift of bread and wine.

On the two names Ellicott cites the Jewish historian for righteous king and the Alexandrian for king of peace. Clarke adds a rabbinic gloss, that the name means the justifier of those who dwell in him, true enough of Christ but false of the city to which the rabbins applied it; on the city he reports that Salem is generally understood to be Jerusalem though some take it for Shechem, where Ellicott says Jewish tradition affirms the site strongly. Wesley draws the moral of the pair, that in him as in Christ righteousness and peace were joined, and so they are in all who believe. The tithe then raises a practical question and divides them. Gill denies that any obligation follows from it, the act being voluntary, done once and not yearly, and taken out of an enemy's spoils rather than his own substance or the increase of the earth; Clarke denies it as well, holding that neither this act nor the like custom of other nations has anything to do with tithes as prescribed under Moses or claimed under Christianity. Barnes infers the contrary, that the propriety of devoting a tenth to God was recognised as a duty before the Levitical law existed, piety having early fixed on that proportion as no more than fitting.
3:
What the threefold negation denies is the crux of the chapter. Gill refers it to the priesthood rather than the person, his father being no priest and his mother of no priestly descent, and he himself having neither predecessor nor successor; or else to his scriptural rather than his natural being, since as a mere man he doubtless had parents of whom Scripture makes no mention. Barnes shows that the word bears several ordinary senses, none of which can be intended here, the point being the absence of a genealogical table. Ellicott makes the third term govern the other two: he is called fatherless not because his parents happen to go unmentioned but because he is introduced suddenly as priest without any token of holding the office by descent, the only claim familiar to Hebrew readers. Calvin goes further: the Spirit is silent as to his birth and records no death, and is not this the same as though eternity were ascribed to him? He adds that in a matter concerning Christ we ought to know nothing but what is written. Robertson agrees the argument is from silence and then cools it markedly: it is not to be pressed, the likeness lies in the picture drawn in Genesis and not in the man, and such interpretation does not amount to proof but serves only as a parallel. He and Ellicott both record that many have from the first been dissatisfied and have read the words as ascribing a superhuman existence.

Clarke states the apologetic purpose plainly. The objection was that a true priest must come of a legitimate stock as every priest under the law did, and that Jesus did not; the answer is that Melchizedek was priest of the most high God and yet of neither Abraham's line nor Aaron's, being, as Clarke says outright, a Canaanite. Wesley draws a christological distinction of his own, that the Son of God is really without father as to his human nature and without mother as to his divine, and in this also without pedigree. Gill adds the antiquarian curiosity that the Arabic writers supply the parents Scripture omits, one of them making Peleg the father.

On the greatness that follows Ellicott prefers the present tense, the greatness abiding as set forth in Scripture, and notes that the tenth was taken from the choicest part of the spoils, a point Barnes makes from the word itself, which means the top of the heap. Robertson calls the adjective one of magnitude rather than number. Henry states the conclusion the argument drives at, that the high priest of whom Melchizedek was a type must be far superior to the Levitical priests, and dwells on Abraham's happiness in having the promises. A difficulty then arises about the Levites. Ellicott states it: the tithe was paid to the Levites, and only a tenth of that reached the priests. He answers it twice, that the question is one of position rather than emolument, and that the Levites themselves paid tithes to the priests, who thus alone received tithes and paid none. Clarke gives the same explanation of the tenth of the tenth. Calvin declines it, holding there is no reason to confine so general a declaration that way, and would rather render the clause because they are the sons of Levi. On the blessing Calvin sets out the principle that the less is blessed by the greater and observes that the more glorious Abraham is made the higher Melchizedek's dignity appears; Ellicott and Robertson both note the perfect tenses, which present what is recorded not as past but as standing now in the ever-present word; and Wesley remarks that where the singular promise is used of Christ, the plural here takes in other blessings besides.
7:
The principle about blessing is admitted by all, and carefully fenced. Barnes limits both terms: the less means one of inferior rank and the better one of superior office, and neither implies anything about purity or holiness of character, since that is not the point in hand. Clarke cites Macknight to the same effect, that the blessing meant is not the simple wishing of good, which inferiors may do to superiors, but the action of one authorised to declare God's intention to bestow good things. Calvin adds the command in Numbers that the priest bless the people, with a promise attached, from which he concludes that such a blessing was not so much man's as God's, and notes that it could never be returned. Gill draws the conclusion, that Melchizedek was therefore greater than Abraham and than the Levites who sprang from him, and Christ his antitype greater still; Ellicott observes that the writer did not think it necessary to state that conclusion at all, Robertson calls the sentence a parenthetical generalisation, and Wesley reduces it to a word, that the blessing is authoritative.

In what sense Melchizedek lives is the harder question. Calvin takes the silence about his death as evidence of life, allows that this would not hold of anyone else, and rests it on his being a type; he then rejects as childish the notion that the man who met Abraham is still alive, the words being applicable to the person he represented. Barnes attacks the opposite evasion, that the contrast is merely between a changing priesthood and an unchanging one; such a reading, he says, would never have occurred to anyone but for the difficulty in the other half of the verse, and does not escape it either. Clarke and Ellicott take a middle course, that he is represented as living because Scripture records neither his death nor any successor, Ellicott adding that under the law men enter by birth into a state carrying the right to tithes and pass out of it by death, whereas here what he holds he holds by personal right.

The apology that follows is agreed to be a softener. Barnes reports the judgment that it amounts to an indirect apology for an unexpected assertion, and Clarke lists the classical authors in whom the idiom is common. What it softens they take differently. Gill and Clarke read the claim as seminal inclusion, Gill drawing the parallel that all mankind were in the loins of Adam when he sinned and fell. Barnes expressly denies three constructions, that Levi actually paid, since he did not then exist; that Abraham was his appointed representative, since Levi appointed no one; and that the act was imputed to him; and offers instead the analogy of a father who sells an estate to which the son would be heir. Robertson is cooler still, calling the whole a rabbinical imaginative refinement that would appeal to Jews. Ellicott finds no real difficulty once it is granted that pre-eminence depended on descent alone. Calvin raises the objection nobody else raises, that Judah, of whose seed Christ came, paid tithes in Abraham on the same reckoning, and answers it twice: Christ is not simply one of Abraham's sons but exempted by a peculiar privilege, as he showed when he asked how David could call his own son Lord; and a type is not to be set against its reality. Wesley puts the same point briefly, that Levi paid not in person but in his successors.
11:
Chrysostom marks the turn. Having shown how far Melchizedek exceeded Abraham, the writer leaves the persons and contends on the ground of the priesthood, finding his force in the circumstance that looked fatal to the claim. Why not after the order of Aaron? From the thing which naturally excluded Christ's priesthood he establishes it; for had Christ come first and the law after, the later might be said to annul the former, but Christ comes later and on a different type, which shows the others imperfect. Clarke defines perfection most fully: the accomplishment of that for which a priesthood is established, an acceptable service, pardon, a conscience purged, a soul prepared for heaven, none of which came by the Levitical law, that being the shadow and not the substance, imperfect in itself though representing a perfect system. Barnes notes that the Jews held the system perfect and permanent, and that the defect is not here specified. Robertson says only that the priesthood failed to give men a perfectly adequate relation to God. Ellicott renders the other priest a priest of a different kind. Wesley reduces it to a phrase, whether this answered all God's designs and man's wants.

The parenthesis about the law carries the argument into the next verse. Calvin lays down the truth on which all turns, that no covenant between God and man is in force and ratified except it rests on a priesthood; the law was introduced under the Levitical priesthood and not merely during it, the priesthood being instituted to confirm the law, so that when one falls the other falls with it. Henry states the consequence, that a new priesthood must be under a new regulation, by rules proper to its own order. How far the change reaches is disputed. Calvin restricts it to what peculiarly belonged to Moses, the part subordinate to the ancient priesthood, insisting that the rule of life and the gratuitous covenant of life were not abolished. Barnes restricts it differently: it cannot touch the ten commandments, given before the priesthood existed, nor any part of the moral law, but only the code regulating the priests and their rites. Clarke puts the essence of the Levitical law in its sacrificial offerings, which could not purge the heart, and so must fall by God's own order. Gill goes furthest: the priesthood was not translated but utterly abolished, everlasting being limited as such words often are.

The proof is then drawn not from the psalm but from its fulfilment. Ellicott sets out the order: verse eleven asserts the other priest, verse twelve shows what so serious a fact carries with it, and here it is substantiated from Jesus; compared with Levi every tribe was not merely one more but essentially a different tribe. Barnes and Clarke agree that no man of Judah had part in the altar. Gill collects the evidence that Jesus sprang from Judah, from Bethlehem and from Joseph and Mary of the house of David, and that the Jews expect Messiah from that tribe and own Jesus was near to the kingdom. Calvin gives the reason the argument runs this way: he speaks to men who confessed Jesus to be the Christ, and since the promised one could derive his origin from no other, they had to be persuaded he was David's son. Clarke rests it on the genealogies: whatever difficulties we find in them now, none were apprehended then, or the enemies of the gospel would have urged them. Wesley says the same in a line, that it was then clear beyond dispute. Ellicott alone hesitates over the verb: everywhere else in the New Testament it is used of the sun rising, but it also denotes the springing up of plants, and a closely connected word stands in the prophecy of the Branch, which he thinks much more suitable here. Robertson keeps the commoner sense.
15:
Barnes guards the opening clause: what is more evident is not that our Lord sprang from Judah but the point being established, that the priesthood must change; and the order proves it more strongly than the tribe, since Melchizedek belonged to that tribe not at all. Calvin marks the shift of ground, that the argument ran before on the person of the priest and now runs on the nature of the priesthood: the ancient had to do with external rites, in Christ's there is nothing but what is spiritual, whence the one was temporary and the other perpetual. Clarke adds that Melchizedek was priest and king together, an office no Levitical priest sustained, though priest, king and prophet all meet in our Lord. Robertson notes the piled-up Greek, a comparative and a still set upon an adjective already thoroughly clear. Wesley states it plainly: the priest now raised up is of a quite different order.

On the carnal commandment the voices converge and then divide over a caution. Ellicott takes it as a commandment of flesh, limited to the sphere of man's fleshly nature, bound up with distinctions of race and tribe, hedged by sickness and death, and therefore temporary; against the enactment he sets an essential right, so that because he lives, in virtue of what he is, Christ is priest. Barnes says the law under which the old priests were made was external rather than spiritual, concerned with outward observance rather than the heart. Robertson insists on the exact word, fleshen and not fleshlike, the Levitical priests becoming such merely by birth. Clarke enters the caution that carnal here does not mean sinful or corrupt but feeble and frail, what may be said of man in his present dying condition. Calvin enters a caution of his own: the old priesthood is called carnal because it worked by ointment, vestments and sprinkled blood, yet it was not so carnal but that it was still spiritual, the contrast here concerning only Christ and Aaron. Gill will only say that Christ was made a priest neither as man nor as God but by appointment.

The proof text is then recited. Gill refers the testifying to David as penman or rather to the Holy Ghost as author, and Ellicott prefers the reading that makes it witness borne to him. Calvin puts the whole weight on the one word for ever, and answers the Jewish objection that the Hebrew need not mean eternity, since Moses uses it of ordinances that have plainly ceased: applied to the ancient sacrifices it reaches no further than the coming of Christ, under whom the world was renovated, but applied to Christ no end can be found. Cyril takes the verse another way, that our Lord is called by two names, Jesus because he saves and Christ because he is a priest, Moses foreshadowing both when he renamed his successor Jesus and surnamed his brother Aaron Christ. Of the disannulling Gill and Barnes agree it touches only the ceremonial commandment, the moral law being unabrogable since it grows out of the nature of things. Robertson finds the word common in the papyri for making void. Clarke says the old law had no energy and furnished no assistance. Calvin traces its weakness to the ceremonies having nothing substantial in themselves, all their virtue derived from Christ, and adds that former laws are abrogated by the latter. Clarke calls what came after a superintroduction set against the preceding commandment, and reads the drawing near as a priestly phrase, the high priest alone approaching once a year and with blood, where now all believers enter by it. Calvin is peculiar, taking the Law itself for the introduction, a preparation like the elements taught to children. Wesley presses it furthest, so nigh as to be one spirit with him, and this is true perfection.
20:
The weight of this section rests on a clause nobody had yet touched. Ellicott notes that these three verses form one sentence, the third answering to the first and the middle one parenthetical, and that the remarkable opening of the psalm so often quoted has been passed over until now; the word used is very uncommon and means the swearing of an oath rather than the oath. Robertson observes only that the negative of the first verse becomes positive in the second. Barnes states the contrast: the Levitical priests received the office by descent and entered on it as a matter of course, whereas Jesus received his by special appointment and had it secured by an oath, which is much more solemn. Wesley reduces it to a sentence, that the greater solemnity proves the superior excellency of the priesthood and shows it unchangeable.

Clarke does not argue the point himself but adopts a long note of Macknight's, which he calls judicious. Its principle is that God never interposed his oath except to show the certainty and immutability of the thing sworn, and it collects the instances: to Abraham that in his seed all nations should be blessed, to the rebellious Israelites that they should not enter his rest, to Moses that he should not enter Canaan, to David that his seed should endure. Hence the oath showed God's immutable resolution never to change Christ's priesthood, nor the covenant established upon it, whereas the Levitical priesthood, established without an oath, was thereby declared changeable at God's pleasure. Clarke adds his own limit to the for ever, that it runs until the mediatorial kingdom is superseded by the fixed state of eternity. Calvin runs the same argument to a different terminus, that the honour of the oath marks the excellence of the covenant rather than of the priest alone, since a priest is made in order to be surety of a covenant. Gill supplies the detail that no oath was used when Aaron and his sons were installed, and reports the later practice by which, after the Sadducees arose, the high priest swore on the day of atonement to change none of its customs; but he sets it aside, since it concerned the execution of the office and not the investiture, and was the priest's own oath and not the Lord's.

What Jesus is surety of, and to whom, is disputed. Barnes takes the word from common life, where a friend pledges name or property that a contract will be met, and rejects the reading of Crellius that Christ is surety for God, since no such security of the divine faithfulness is needed or possible; the suretyship runs the other way, on the part of man, and extends to this, that the law shall be honoured and its demands met so that the penalty does not fall on those who violated it. He adds that it is no suretyship that men shall be saved without holiness, repentance and faith. Robertson leaves open what Barnes closes, saying it is not clear whether Jesus is God's pledge to man or man's to God, and answering that he is in fact both, as Mediator. Clarke reads surety as mediator, one who brings the parties together, witnesses the contract and offers the covenant sacrifice. On the noun that follows, Ellicott presses at length that covenant is the true rendering, tracing how the Greek word rendered a Hebrew term translated covenant more than two hundred times, how classical usage and the old Latin brought in testament, and how Paul's own phrase for the Jewish Scriptures came by that route to be the Old Testament. Wesley grants the word bears both senses. Gill will have both at once, a testament as bequeathing an inheritance confirmed by the death of the testator, and a covenant as a compact made with Christ as representative of the elect.
23:
The contrast is between a succession and a single holder. Robertson fixes the comparative, more than one and in succession rather than simultaneously, hindered by death from continuing. Ellicott renders it that they have been made priests many in number because death prevented their continuance, recalling the earlier contrast between dying men and one who liveth. Barnes puts the ground in the frailty of human nature and the shortness of life. Clarke says only that a succession was necessary because they were mortal men. Gill supplies numbers the others do not, that the Jews reckon eighteen high priests under the first temple and more than three hundred under the second, and reads the multitude itself as proof of imperfection. Calvin notes that he has touched this comparison already but that the point is now different: before he concluded the ancient priesthood must end because its holders were mortal, whereas here he shows only that Christ remains perpetually a priest.

Over the adjective in the next verse there is a genuine division. Barnes prefers the marginal rendering, that the priesthood does not pass from one to another, the idea being not strictly unchangeableness but that it does not pass into other hands, since what moved it among the Levites was not failure but mortality. Ellicott takes it as inviolable and doubts whether the Greek will bear the marginal meaning at all: since his life is indissoluble, none can trespass on his right and invade his priesthood. Robertson agrees, glossing the word valid or inviolate. Wesley keeps the marginal sense in three words, that it passes to no successor, and Clarke has it both ways. Barnes then enters a limitation nobody else makes, that the reasoning is not designed to prove the priesthood literally eternal, since its necessity may cease when all the redeemed are in heaven. Gill meets the obvious objection, that Christ did die: death did not forbid him to continue as it does other men, he died voluntarily, continued but a small time under its power, and his death was itself a branch of his priestly office.

How the uttermost should be read divides them much as the Latin divided them. Robertson reports that the Vulgate takes it temporally but that the common meaning is completely or utterly. Calvin's own version follows the Vulgate and reads for ever, though his editor observes that the original refers not to time but to what is fully done, citing Erasmus, Beza, Capellus and Schleusner, and asks further whether the phrase attaches to able or to save; most join it to save, but since the subject is the perfection of Christ as a priest rather than the character of the salvation, it should go with able. Barnes takes the same side against a temporal sense, the word meaning a salvation which is complete, so that he does not begin a work he cannot finish. Clarke will have both, to all intents and purposes and also through all times, the second being his preference because of the clause that follows. Wesley names what it covers, the guilt, power, root and consequence of sin, and Gill what the work required, a law fulfilled, justice satisfied, sin borne and enemies met, none of which any creature could undertake. On the intercession Barnes is most cautious, admitting that the precise mode is not revealed and understanding it as the constant presentation of the merits of the death. Clarke sets out six senses the verb can carry and adopts Macknight's inference that Christ's living must mean living in the body. Ellicott ties it to the high priest's confession on the day of atonement and to the incense, Calvin to the people standing in the court while one man entered the sanctuary, where now no veil intervenes. Robertson borrows Moffatt's phrase, that this intercession has red blood in it, unlike the conception of Philo.
26:
The fitness of such a priest to such people is put by several as a paradox, and by Wesley barest: such a high priest suited us, unholy, mischievous, defiled sinners, a blessed paradox. Clarke lists the five qualifications required of the Jewish high priest, applies them to Christ in a higher sense, and sets the antithesis plainly, that he was holy and we unholy, harmless and we harmful. Barnes locates the necessity in us: it was not enough that our priest have great power or a rank above the Levitical, since our character demanded moral purity in him. Gill says only that such a priest answers our cases and necessities. Henry describes the purity itself, that Christ has not the least disposition to sin in his nature, whereas such inclination dwells in the best of Christians. Calvin reads Aaron's costly vestments as symbols of a holiness far exceeding human virtues, introduced because the reality did not exist, and distributes the terms, holy toward God, harmless toward men, undefiled as to himself, separate in being removed elsewhere; Christ is not called separate, he adds, because he repels us from his society but because he alone is free from stain.

On that word they divide. Ellicott sets out both constructions: joined to what precedes, it marks the sinlessness of one who lived among sinners without needing external separation from pollution; joined to what follows, it marks the severance that now exists, our exalted Lord being removed for ever from a life among transgressors. He judges the first more probable; Robertson takes the second, referring the participle to the exaltation, and prefaces his adjectives with Moffatt's warning that it is misleading to parse a rhapsody. Ellicott alone supplies the ritual behind the language, that seven days before the day of atonement the high priest left his house and lodged in the temple, with five washings and ten purifications on the day itself.

The daily offering in the next verse is a real difficulty, and Ellicott alone says so. The annual day of atonement is what the language naturally suits, and neither the morning and evening sacrifices nor the high priest's daily meat-offering can be so described; so either the word means each recurrence of that sacred day, or it attaches not to the Jewish high priests but to Jesus alone, which the Greek order would suggest. Wesley takes the first way without noticing the difficulty. Barnes and Clarke take the plainer road, that there was a daily sacrifice on the high priest's behalf, Barnes granting he did not personally officiate at it, Clarke reporting that the Jews held a priest who neglected it would be smitten with death. Calvin reduces the same material to two defects, that the priest offered for his own sins and so could not pacify God for others, and that the offering was repeated, whence there was no real expiation, since sins remain when purgation repeats.

The last verse turns on the order of the two appointments. Clarke dates it, that David wrote nearly five hundred years after the law, so that the oath constituting another priesthood abrogates it. Ellicott says it more compactly, that the oath, coming after the law, revoked the commandment and was not itself revoked by it, and enters a caution the others do not, that Jesus is not to be understood as first perfected and then appointed, since it was as high priest that he offered himself. Calvin draws the rule that in the institutions of God what comes later either advances the former or abolishes what was to last only a time. Robertson notes that the closing words bind two psalms. Barnes glosses the last participle as perfected and takes the appointment to be complete and permanent, while Gill and Wesley set the contrast in the word infirmity, which Gill insists means not bodily blemish, barred by law, but sinful weakness.
